question: The three policies from the last experiment fail only because the gripper command goes past its limit. If we clip the gripper command to its exact limits at run time, with no retraining, do they pass 15/15 with zero safety frames?
measure: Clean successes out of 15 rollouts and safety frames per seed, for the same three trained policies with and without the clip.
outcome: Seeds 101 and 202 passed: 15/15 with zero safety frames, the first policies in the repository to do so. Seed 303 stayed at 12/15 with 9 safety frames, on the three frames that were named as a risk before the run.
setup: A policy is the network that drives the arm. The teacher is a hand-written script that does the task using the cube's exact position from the simulator; the policy is trained to copy the teacher's recorded commands. The policy outputs a chunk: the next 90 commands at once. A seed is the random number that starts training; the same recipe with a different seed gives a different policy. The test is called Stage A: 5 scenarios (the nominal cube position and four positions shifted by 1.5 mm), 3 repeats each, 15 rollouts. A rollout is one full attempt. A safety frame is one step where the policy asks a joint to leave its allowed range (a clip) or to move faster than the per-step cap (a limit). A rollout with any safety frame does not count. To pass, a policy needs 15 of 15 with zero safety frames. The previous experiment trained three seeds on a full 480-step recording. They scored 9, 9 and 12 out of 15. Every bad frame was the gripper. Most were clips: the policy asked for a gripper value below the closed limit (0.000472), by 0.002 to 0.02, while squeezing the cube during set-down. Seed 303 also had three limit frames (steps 413 to 415): the gripper opening faster than the per-step cap during release. The fix tested here is a clamp: at the point where each command leaves the policy, clip the gripper channel to its exact allowed range. Only the gripper is clamped, because clamping the other joints to their raw bounds trips the clip check on shoulder lift and elbow flex through float32 rounding. This is an evaluation-only change. The weights are the same files, checked by hash.

parts.title: Does clipping the gripper output turn the three policies into passing ones?
parts.why: Retraining had not removed the overshoot, and the overshoot was larger than any margin the training targets could hold. A clip removes out-of-range gripper commands by construction, so it should fix every seed whose only problem is the range.
parts.did: Re-ran Stage A on the three existing checkpoints with the gripper channel clamped. No training. About 14 minutes.

predictions.text: Seeds 101 and 202 pass (their violations are all gripper clips, which the clamp removes by construction)
Primary prediction: all three seeds pass
Registered risk: if seed 303 fails, it fails on exactly its three limit frames at steps 413 to 415

parts.conclusion: Two of three seeds pass with zero safety frames. Under the strict rule (all three must pass) the gate status is clamp_not_resolved. The clamp removed every clip violation at zero training cost.

parts.title: Why does seed 303 still fail?
parts.why: The proposal said in advance that the clamp cannot remove limit frames directly. They could only vanish if the slightly different trajectory under the clamp happened to avoid them.
parts.did: Ran the frame analysis on the failing seed 303 evaluation.
parts.conclusion: The only violations left are the same three frames, in one scenario (cube_y_minus), repeated identically in its 3 repeats: 9 safety frames and 3 lost rollouts. The gripper opens faster than the per-step cap. A range clip does nothing about speed, and the changed trajectory did not dissolve them. The excess values are the same as before the clamp.

trust.text: Same three checkpoints as the baseline rows, validated by checkpoint hash against the earlier gate report. Nothing was retrained.
Same Stage A test and pass rule as every earlier gate.
The prediction, the seed 303 risk and the statuses were written down before the run.
Checked before the run that a command exactly on the gripper bound does not count as a clip (the test uses a strict inequality).
The clamp is legal only on the gripper channel. A general clamp would need an inward margin and was not tested.
Three seeds, five scenarios within 1.5 mm, simulation only, cube position read from the simulator.
The gate's formal status is clamp_not_resolved, because one seed fails. The record's 'worked' reflects the 2 of 3 seeds.

meaning: The last failure of the state policies (policies that read the cube position from the simulator) was narrow enough to fix at run time. The clamp became a standard part of every later policy, including the vision policies. Per the plan written before the run, tuning of the state policy stopped here regardless of the outcome, and the project moved to the vision rung: replacing the cube position with the wrist camera. The one open defect is seed 303 opening the gripper too fast for three frames. The note names a candidate fix, a per-step speed limit on the gripper output, for a later pass.
lesson: Once a failure is narrow and pinned to one channel, the cheapest fix at run time can beat more retraining. Writing the expected partial outcome down first is what made the seed 303 failure a confirmation and not a surprise.

log:
**TL;DR:** Clipping the gripper command to its limits at run time, with no
retraining, gave the first 15/15 with zero safety frames in the project, on two
of three seeds.

**Problem.** The policies overshot the gripper past its closed limit (entry 13).

*How we know:* for two of the seeds, every single violation was the gripper
going below its floor. I didn't know if fixing just that would be enough.

**Experiment.** Re-run the same three trained policies, but clip the gripper
output to its exact limits before sending it. Only the gripper: clipping the
other joints trips rounding errors. Written down beforehand: seeds 101 and 202
should pass, and 303 might not, because its 3 bad frames per try were the
gripper opening too fast, not going past a limit.

*What we hope to learn:* whether this one narrow failure is the whole story.

**Outcome.** Exactly as predicted:

| seed | result | safety frames |
|---|---|---|
| 101 | 15/15 | 0 |
| 202 | 15/15 | 0 |
| 303 | 12/15 | 9 |

- The clip removes any out-of-range command by construction, so the over-squeeze
  just disappears. It does nothing about speed, though. Like a fence: it stops
  you leaving the yard, not running too fast inside it.

The clip became part of every policy after this.

**Takeaway:** once a failure is narrow and pinned down, the cheapest fix at run
time can beat any amount of retraining. And writing the partial outcome down
first means you know it's real when it shows up.
